## OPEN
A: From Void News, this is On Air. It's Friday, September eighteenth. Canada has answered Washington's tariff threat by moving toward Europe.

## MENU
A: On the desk today.
A: Canada's prime minister embraces a first-of-its-kind seat at the European table.
B: The Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time in three years.
A: A federal judge orders thirty days' notice before anyone touches the Kennedy Center.
B: Venezuela moves closer to bringing four billion dollars of gold home.
A: Pentagon staff have a nickname for the defense secretary's wife.

## STORY 1 | Canada turns toward Europe
A: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed a proposal to make Canada the European Union's first associate member. The offer comes from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Carney raised it himself during an official trip that took him from the United Kingdom to Brussels.
A: Carney says closer ties with Europe would stop any single country from controlling Canada's markets or undermining its sovereignty. He made the case in person to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday. He told lawmakers an alliance with Europe is a choice about who Canada wants to depend on.
A: The timing is the story. U-S President Donald Trump has called the idea a hostile act. He has threatened tariffs, and he has raised the prospect of a trade embargo against the E-U itself. Ottawa has not withdrawn the request.
A: Coverage splits on what the move means. Reuters and The Hill report the speech and the application as a diplomatic step. Al Jazeera and The Spectator ask whether Canada will come to regret tying its trade future to Brussels.
B: Canada has also applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force, a British-led defense grouping of northern European states.

## STORY 2 | The Fed raises rates
B: To the markets. The Federal Reserve has raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point. It is the first increase in three years. The target range now sits between three and three-quarter percent and four percent.
B: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh says inflation is too high and has been for too long. He says the increase is meant to bring prices back to the central bank's two percent target sooner. The latest consumer price index shows prices up almost half a percent in a month and just under three and a half percent over the year.
B: Oil and gas have been doing much of the pushing. The Fed points to the situation in Iran and elsewhere for the climb in fuel costs. Its preferred inflation gauge, which tracks personal spending, is also still rising.
A: Some outlets lead instead with President Trump's reaction, and with a private phone call between the president and the Fed chairman before the decision.

## STORY 3 | Kennedy Center gets thirty days
A: In Washington, a federal judge has ordered the Kennedy Center's board to give thirty days' notice before any major physical change to the building, demolition included. Judge Christopher Cooper issued the order on Thursday. It reinforces an earlier injunction that blocked the center from closing for its planned renovation.
A: The court also wants a detailed status report on the temporary closure and the emergency repairs, backed by a sworn statement from someone who knows the building. The center's main hall has been shut on what the board calls public safety grounds, citing structural deterioration.
A: The order follows a photograph. President Trump was pictured on Wednesday night with what appeared to be plans to demolish the center. He says the building will end up ripped down if his administration does not get recognition for the renovation.
B: The framing differs by outlet. The Daily Beast and C-N-N describe the president's remarks as threats, while RedState presents the closure as a matter of safety and renewal.

## STORY 4 | Venezuela's gold comes home
B: To South America. Venezuela is close to a deal to move four billion dollars of gold from the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It would end a legal dispute that has run almost eight years. Acting President Delcy Rodriguez and the opposition agreed in August to recover the metal, about thirty-one tonnes of it.
B: Control would be legal rather than practical. The interim government would gain title to the gold, but not the right to sell it, with the reserve supervised and restricted. The plan is to use it as collateral for reconstruction borrowing after June's earthquakes, which killed more than six thousand people and caused almost twenty billion dollars in damage.
B: The diplomacy is moving too. President Trump is preparing for a first meeting with Rodriguez at the U-N General Assembly in New York. The White House has also removed Venezuela from its list of major drug transit countries for the coming fiscal year.
A: Semafor and Mother Jones report that U-S oil companies, among them Chevron and Continental Resources, are signing or nearing deals in Venezuela.

## BRIEFS
A: Also on the desk.
A: Pentagon staff have taken to calling the defense secretary's wife Yoko Ono, and a spokesperson calls Jennifer Hegseth a force multiplier.
A: A suicide attack on a police compound in Kohat, in northwest Pakistan, has killed at least twenty-one people and injured more than eighty.
B: Robert Kraft says he is banning Macklemore from two Ed Sheeran shows at Gillette Stadium over dangerous lies, not free speech.
B: Radio host Sid Rosenberg, a critic of J-D Vance on Israel, says the vice president won him over in a meeting on Thursday.
A: The Kremlin has placed the Russian operations of Nestle and three French companies under temporary state administration.
A: The White House has withdrawn Lance Schroyer's nomination to run Immigration and Customs Enforcement after both parties questioned his qualifications.
B: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has cancelled his trip to the U-N as a new poll finds almost half of Germans expect him gone by year's end.
B: French President Emmanuel Macron says Russian hybrid attacks on France have intensified and has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure.

## FINALLY | 15 | Hong Kong hires an AI chief
B: One more before Void Opinion. Hong Kong plans to recruit a chief artificial intelligence officer by the middle of next year. The government says it is confident the local talent pool can fill the post. The job would sit at the top of the city's push to turn research into industry, and the search starts now.

## CLOSE
A: That's On Air from Void News. Thirty-one tonnes of gold, and a court order that buys the Kennedy Center thirty days. Every source, every story, at Void News.
